transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 1h18m
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (Redwood Infra), Ravi Sinha (Redwood PM); Maya Chen (CTO), Luis Martinez (ML Infra), Anika Solberg (Security), Devon Park (NLP Eng), Sofia Alvarez (SRE)

Summary: Deep technical session focused on long-context (128k+ token) performance, KV cache behavior for extremely long sequences, chunking/streaming strategies, attention pruning/optimizations, batching tradeoffs, quantization sensitivity, and constraints for VPC/on-prem deployments. Customer provided high-level KPIs: 1) sustained throughput for batched inference on 128k+ contexts, 2) median p99 latency goals for interactive augmentation flows, 3) strong encryption and KMS integration for on-prem pilot.

Topics: long-context memory, prefix/KV caching, continuous batching, chunking to disk vs memory, attention window sliding, quantization (INT8/FP16/bf16), kernel selection, Tensor Core utilization, VPC networking, HSM/KMS, SOC2 docs, pilot scope.

[00:00] Jordan: OK hey everyone thanks for taking the time, we wanted to do a focused session to go through the 128k+ flows you mentioned in the RFI, and talk about how Redwood handles KV cache, batching, and quantization on Dedicated and Private deployments.
[00:18] Maya: Thanks Jordan. We ran into a couple of surprises when we tried longer-context runs internally, like memory blowups and some unstable p99 spikes, so want to understand engineering tradeoffs.
[00:28] Priya: Totally. Quick note: I'll jump into kernel-level stuff, batching heuristics and quantization effects. Jordan will cover deployment and next steps.
[00:35] Luis: For context, our typical query is a 120-160k token user context plus a 2k prompt, so we care about both throughput for batch inference and tail latency for interactive sessions where a user is doing retrieval-augmented generation.
[00:50] Priya: Understood. First thing: KV cache we use continuous prefix caching, but at 128k you have two main levers - sharded KV across GPUs vs pinned big-KV on NVMe with memory-mapped prefetching. With sharding you keep everything in-GPU memory but need cross-GPU sync; with NVMe-backed KV you trade latency for capacity.
[01:10] Devon: When you say "prefetching" are you referring to our own prefetch layer or Redwood's auto-prefetch logic?
[01:15] Priya: Redwood runtime has an auto-prefetcher that monitors access patterns and tries to keep hot KV in GPU DRAM. It's heuristics-based: LRU-ish but aware of recency patterns for sliding-window attention. For Aurora's workload we'd likely tune the hot-set threshold aggressively.
[01:30] Luis: We saw some transcripts where the model re-attends to earlier sections so the access pattern isn't strictly sliding window, it's more a wandering attention.
[01:38] Priya: Right, the wandering attention breaks naive sliding-window assumptions. There we recommend a hybrid: keep the most recent N tokens cached on-GPU and maintain a bloom-filtered index for cold KV on NVMe to reduce fetch cost.
[01:50] Oliver: On the runtime side, kernel choice matters a lot. For attention we pick fused attention kernels when sequence length fits in kernel memory; for extreme lengths we switch to chunked attention kernels with recomputation to reduce peak memory. That increases compute and latency but keeps it feasible.
[02:10] Maya: Can you quantify how much latency increases when switching from fused to chunked attention? Ballpark.
[02:15] Priya: Ballpark: for an attention op that was 50ms fused at 32k it might become 120-150ms chunked at 128k depending on batch size and sequence shape. The biggest win is when you can amortize recompute across many tokens with batching.
[02:30] Luis: Speaking of batching, we want to run multi-tenant batches. How does Redwood balance batching for throughput without blowing up p99 for interactive flows?
[02:40] Jordan: We use a two-queue routing system: interactive queue with strict latency SLO that uses smaller micro-batches and warm KV-friendly routing; and background throughput queue that allows larger batches. Requests get routed by policy; you can pin a model version and a routing policy per route.
[02:55] Sofia: Does that routing add head-of-line blocking?
[02:58] Jordan: We have adaptive admission and non-blocking priority lanes; with backpressure we can preempt or spin up burst capacity if Dedicated pool allows it. There's metrics to tune the tradeoff.
[03:10] Devon: What about tokenization and chunking strategies? We assume chunk boundaries need to align to sentence boundaries to reduce context jumps.
[03:18] Priya: For RAG use-cases we prefer overlap-chunking with a sliding overlap (e.g., 1-2k tokens) and an index that maps document chunks to KV pointers. Overlap reduces boundary effects but increases KV size. Compression and dedup (hash-based) help.
[03:33] Luis: Have you tried compressed KV entries? Like storing quantized KV or sparse encodings?
[03:37] Priya: Yes, quantized KV is a thing — storing KV in INT8 or 4-bit packs on NVMe is possible. We also support mixed: store keys in FP16 for lookup accuracy, values in INT8. That reduces read/write sizes but costs extra conversion CPU cycles.
[03:52] Maya: Does that change model quality on re-generation? Any measured delta?
[03:55] Priya: Small deltas. In our internal tests on a few open LLMs, INT8 for KV values caused a ~0.3-0.8% token-level perplexity degradation depending on architecture and whether attention is sensitive. We always recommend a small eval run with your prompt set.
[04:12] Ravi: Kernel-level optimization question: are you using Tensor Cores and fused-matmul when possible?
[04:18] Oliver: Yep. For FP16/bf16 we target Tensor Cores with custom fused kernels. For INT8 we use quantized matmul paths with calibration tables. The runtime picks kernels based on model shape, sequence length, and hardware topology.
[04:32] Luis: For our on-prem racks we have A100-ish and some H100s. Any guidance on which is better for 128k?
[04:40] Priya: H100 has better sparsity and on-chip memory for certain kernels, but A100 with more aggregate GPU memory sometimes simplifies KV-in-GPU approaches. If you want to avoid NVMe-backed KV, choose GPUs with large HBM and scale horizontally with sharded KV. H100 helps if you plan on INT8 with sparsity.
[04:58] Anika: Security question: if we keep KV on NVMe in a private deployment, how is that encrypted and how do we ensure keys are stored in our KMS?
[05:06] Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. NVMe volumes are encrypted at rest; we can configure keys to be retrieved from your HSM and never persist in Redwood control plane. We also provide audit logs for KV access.
[05:20] Anika: Good. Also need to ensure we have RBAC around ability to spin up Dedicated nodes in VPC.
[05:25] Jordan: That's supported; SSO + RBAC + allowed-subnet enforcement. We will share the security checklist and the private deployment runbook.
[05:35] Devon: Back to batching — do you do dynamic batching or fixed batch windows?
[05:40] Priya: Dynamic batching. The runtime monitors latency budgets per route and will grow batch sizes opportunistically. For interactive routes we enforce a max waiting time (e.g., 8-12ms) to cap added latency. For throughput routes we allow larger windows and schedule batches when fullness hits threshold.
[05:55] Luis: What about KV eviction policies when upstream writes push KV size beyond expected? We can't just OOM.
[06:02] Priya: Eviction policy is hierarchical: first try local non-critical caches, then cold-migrate to NVMe, then evict LRU from NVMe if necessary. We also support offload-to-object-store for archival of very old KV. You can tune the hot-set percent and eviction thresholds.
[06:18] Maya: For our use-case, sometimes the model re-halls earlier doc sections for rare lookups; do you support partial recomputation or on-the-fly rematerialization?
[06:27] Priya: Yes, rematerialization helps: if you kept a checkpointed intermediate KV snapshot at regular intervals you can recompute the dense KV for the small segment needed instead of storing everything. It's a compute vs storage trade.
[06:38] Oliver: Also worth noting: our compilation layer can fuse remat and attention patterns for repeated access so the recompute is optimized.
[06:45] Luis: There's a lot here about recompute increasing cost but saving memory. How do we estimate cost?
[06:50] Priya: We provide a cost calculator that simulates the expected KB reads, NVMe bandwidth, extra FLOPs for remat, and translates to perf and cost estimates. We'll run Aurora's sample workload through it for a more accurate projection.
[07:02] Devon: On the topic of quantization — have you seen models with long-context memory become more brittle under aggressive quant? Any heuristics?
[07:10] Priya: Aggressive quant (4-bit) can harm memory retention for older tokens because small representational shifts amplify over many attention steps. Heuristic: quantize attention value vectors conservatively and keep query/key in FP16. Prefer mixed-precision for long-context models.
[07:26] Maya: Could you run a sensitivity sweep against our actual prompt set?
[07:29] Priya: Yes, that's one of the SE action items — we'll run INT8/FP16/mixed sweeps and report token-level deltas and end-to-end latency impacts.
[07:36] [09:12] Speaker 2: (brief crosstalk) yeah that makes sense, sorry interjection, is there a simple knob for us to toggle between NVMe-backed KV and GPU-sharded KV in Redwood Dedicated?
[07:52] Jordan: Yes, it's config flags in the deployment spec. You can define KV mode per model or per route: IN_GPU_SHARD, NVME_BACKED, HYBRID. Each has runtime metrics exposed.
[08:03] Sofia: For monitoring, what telemetry do we get? Token-level latency, KV-hit rate?
[08:09] Oliver: We expose token emission time-series, KV hit/miss rates, NVMe IO rates, kernel time breakdown (attention vs matmul vs softmax), and batching histograms. These are visible in Redwood Console and can stream to your observability stack.
[08:25] Luis: Any special build or kernel we should use for H100s?
[08:29] Priya: We use a tuned kernel set per GPU family. For H100 there's a set that takes advantage of new DPX instructions and sparsity paths; we provide prebuilt images for Private deployments.
[08:41] Maya: What about compiling models that exceed the per-GPU memory for the model weights themselves, not just KV?
[08:46] Oliver: We support tensor sharding (FSDP-like) at the runtime layer for model weights and support offloading optimizer states and activations. For inference we can do tensor-parallel sharding and pipeline across GPUs to host the model. That complexity is hidden from the API but present in the deployment spec.
[09:03] Devon: We are also exploring chunking docs at ingest time to produce smaller semantic windows; how does that interact with your KV pointers?
[09:10] Priya: The index maps chunk ids to base offset in the KV store; chunking at ingest simply increases the number of pointers but reduces per-chunk token length which helps fused kernels. We recommend chunk sizes that keep attention windows under 8-16k where possible for best perf.
[09:27] Luis: If we chunk too aggressively, we risk losing context cohesion. Tradeoff.
[09:31] Priya: Right. Overlap helps and you can do smart chunk boundaries by semantic sentence splits. We have an ingestion pipeline example for that.
[09:40] Anika: For on-prem audit we need proof that NVMe-backed KV is wiped after decommission.
[09:45] Jordan: Wiping, attestations, and HSM key destruction are in the runbook. We'll share the decommission checklist.
[09:55] Maya: Let's talk daily cost numbers. Rough estimate per 1M tokens with our mix of interactive and throughput?
[10:02] Ravi: We actually prepared a very rough model during the call: with hybrid KV, and mixed batching the cost per 1M tokens was X (internal placeholder) — Jordan will send the detailed sheet; the high-level: NVMe reduces capital costs but increases per-token latency and IO cost.
[10:20] Devon: Are there known model families that behave particularly poorly at 128k and we should avoid?
[10:25] Priya: Some decoder-only architectures with very deep cross-attention stacks show super-linear memory growth; also models that use very wide heads can blow up kernel memory. We'll test your chosen model family during the pilot.
[10:36] Luis: We also want to enforce traffic isolation across internal teams on the Dedicated pool. Is there network-level isolation?
[10:43] Jordan: Yes — per-tenant VPCs, subnet restrictions, and private endpoints. We also support mTLS and client cert auth to the runtime endpoints.
[10:53] Anika: For compliance, we need all audit logs for any KV access correlated to request IDs. Is that feasible?
[10:59] Oliver: Yes we can correlate KV read/write events to request IDs and stream to your SIEM. There's a small perf overhead for very high cardinality logging, but it's tunable.
[11:10] Devon: Do you have any recommendations for sequence caching size? We have GPUs with 80GB HBM and NVMe pool per node.
[11:17] Priya: If you have 80GB HBM and plan to run a single model replica, you can keep ~30-50k tokens hot depending on model size. For 128k you either need 3-4 GPUs sharding or NVMe backing. We'll simulate exact numbers.
[11:30] Maya: OK, last big question: when the model needs to attend to tokens 120k tokens back but only rarely, what's the best architecture?
[11:38] Priya: Best architecture: hybrid with checkpointed rematerialization and an index that stores compact representations (compressed KV) for cold segments. On a rare miss, fetch compressed KV, do a small-scale recompute or expansion to full representation, then proceed. That gives the ability to have multi-day histories without constant GPU memory.
[11:58] Luis: Sounds good. For the pilot, the practical asks are: run our sample 150k prompt workload, provide p50/p95/p99 and token throughput, measure KV hit/miss and NVMe IO, and run quantization sensitivity.
[12:10] Jordan: We'll do that. Priya will own quantization sweeps and kernel tuning; Oliver will collect kernel traces; Jordan will share the measurement harness and pricing model.
[12:22] Maya: Thanks. Let's recap next steps.

Recap / Next steps (verbatim):
- Jordan: share benchmark config & measurement harness, and pricing sheet by 2026-03-06.
- Priya: run INT8/FP16/mixed quant sensitivity on Aurora's sample set and share results 2026-03-09.
- Oliver: provide kernel-level trace and metrics and recommended GPU family optimizations by 2026-03-10.
- Luis: upload representative 150k prompt corpus and SLO doc to shared drive by 2026-03-10.
- Anika: confirm compliance must-haves for on-prem pilot, KMS/HSM constraints by 2026-03-08.

Action items repeated here as a short list: Jordan to send benchmark spreadsheet; Priya to run quant sweeps; Oliver to send kernel traces; Luis to provide sample prompts; Anika to confirm compliance constraints.

References mentioned: benchmark config spreadsheet (link sent in chat), Redwood Private deployment runbook (reference), SOC2 attestation pack, sample perf dashboards (Redwood Console), NVMe encryption notes.
